levelAbout.A1: A1 is the first step of the CEFR scale. {language} texts at this level use short sentences and everyday words. Expect to look up many words at first, so read a few pages at a time.
levelAbout.A2: A2 is the elementary level. You know the basics of {language} and can follow simple stories. Texts here use common words and clear sentences, with some new words on each page.
levelAbout.B1: B1 is the intermediate level. You can follow the main story in {language} without help. Expect longer sentences and a wider range of words, and look up only the words you need.
levelAbout.B2: B2 is the upper intermediate level. You can read most {language} stories and articles with ease. Expect rich vocabulary and long sentences. Tap a word for its meaning when a page slows you down.
levelAbout.C1: C1 is the advanced level. You can read long {language} texts and follow ideas that are not stated in plain words. Expect literary style, rare words and long, complex sentences.
levelAbout.C2: C2 is the top of the CEFR scale. These {language} books are the hardest on Readfox: classic literary and philosophical texts. Expect old words, dense prose and long chapters.

publicBooks.featuredIntro: Try the opening pages free in your browser. In the Readfox reader, you can tap unfamiliar words for their meanings.

featuredReasons.contes-du-lundi: Start with “The Last Lesson.” A schoolboy tells the story in the first person, and the classroom setting gives you clues when the older vocabulary is unfamiliar.
featuredReasons.lettres-de-mon-moulin: “Installation” opens with rabbits and an old mill. The concrete setting helps you follow the scene while you meet descriptive words about the countryside.
featuredReasons.la-petite-fadette: Choose this if you want a longer story. The opening follows a farming family, with rural vocabulary and longer sentences for an extra challenge.
featuredReasons.an-elementary-spanish-reader: A chicken thinks the sky is falling. The short sentences, present-tense verbs, and repeated dialogue make the opening easy to follow.
featuredReasons.lecturas-faciles: Start with the fable about a father, his son, and a donkey. The action is easy to picture, and the story is good practice for common past-tense verbs.
featuredReasons.the-wonderful-wizard-of-oz: Start with Dorothy and the cyclone. A familiar plot and concrete descriptions help you keep reading even when a word is new.
featuredReasons.daddy-long-legs: Read for everyday English in a school setting. The narrator opens with a lively account of inspection day before the story moves into letters about college life.
featuredReasons.a-little-princess: Follow Sara’s arrival at a London boarding school. The dialogue gives you a way into the story, and the descriptive prose adds a vocabulary challenge.
